question: Tell me about a project you led.
text: Last year I led a project to move our team's monthly reports from spreadsheets into a shared dashboard. There were four of us, and I set up a weekly check-in and a simple task list so everyone knew who owned what. The hardest part was agreeing on which numbers mattered, so I sat down with each manager and wrote their needs into one page. We launched two weeks early, and the reports now take about half a day instead of three days. I learned that most of the work in a project is making sure people agree before you build anything.

question: Tell me about a project you led.
text: I led a small project at a community health clinic to cut down missed appointments. I looked at six months of booking data and saw that most no-shows were for early morning slots. I worked with the reception team to send text reminders the day before and to offer a call-back option. I also wrote a short guide so new staff could follow the same steps. Within three months missed appointments dropped by about a quarter. It wasn't a big budget project, but it made a real difference for the doctors and the patients.

text: I led the launch of a loyalty program for a chain of three cafes. My job was to choose the system, train staff and track the results. In the first two months we signed up about nine hundred customers, and repeat visits went up. I enjoyed seeing a plan turn into something people used every day.

question: Tell me about a project you led.
text: I led a project to digitise paper records at a small accounting firm. We had about twenty years of client files in boxes. I worked out which files we legally had to keep, set up a naming system, and hired two casual staff to scan them. I checked a sample of each batch to make sure nothing was missing. It took four months, and we cleared an entire storage room that we now use as a meeting space. Finding old files went from taking hours to taking a few seconds.

question: Tell me about a project you led.
text: I led a team of three warehouse staff to set up a new returns process. Returns were piling up because nobody owned them. I created a simple flow: check the item, decide if it can be resold, and record it the same day. I put a whiteboard by the returns bench so everyone could see the backlog. Within a month the backlog was gone, and we were putting more items back on sale instead of writing them off. I think the key was making the process simple enough that anyone could follow it.

text: I led a project to reduce food waste in a hotel kitchen. I started by weighing what we threw away each day for a month and sorting it by type. Waste went down by about thirty percent, and food costs dropped too. It showed me how much you can change once you actually measure something.

text: A customer's delivery kept arriving damaged, three times in a row. Instead of just sending another one, I looked at where the damage was happening. The next delivery arrived in perfect condition, and we applied the same packaging to similar orders. The customer stayed with us, and our damage claims for that product line dropped close to zero.

question: Describe a time you solved a difficult problem.
text: In a lab job, one of our test machines started giving results that drifted over the day. Everyone assumed the machine was faulty. I logged the room temperature next to each result and noticed the drift matched the afternoon heat. We moved the machine away from the window and added a short warm-up and calibration step each morning. The results became stable again, and we avoided buying a new machine, which would have cost a lot. It taught me to check the simple explanations before the expensive ones.

text: At a call centre I worked in, our weekly reports kept showing a spike in complaints on Mondays. After that I started using a short checklist before sending any report, including checking the dates on every table. I haven't made that mistake again, and the checklist has caught a few other errors too.

It taught me that past data is useful, but you have to check what has changed.

question: Tell me about a mistake you made and what you learned.
text: In my first supervisor role, I tried to do too much myself instead of delegating. I was working late, and some tasks slipped. My manager pointed it out, and I realised I didn't trust the team enough. I started giving people clear tasks with deadlines and checking in briefly each day. The team got more done, and two of them later told me they enjoyed having more responsibility. It changed how I think about leading.
